opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I take it seriously. I don't think it's a crazy argument. There are real limitations in current systems. They're still pretty bad at long-horizon agency. They don't learn continually the way a human employee does after a few weeks on the job. They can be weirdly brittle, they hallucinate, and they're less data-efficient than humans by many orders of magnitude.

So I don't dismiss the "we need a new paradigm" view. But I'm skeptical of how it's usually deployed, for a few reasons.

First, people have been saying versions of this for years, and the goalposts keep moving. A while ago the claim was that these models can't really reason, can't do math, can't code beyond toy problems. Then we got reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models, and a lot of those limitations shrank dramatically. You could argue that was itself a new paradigm, or at least a significant new ingredient. That's my second point: even if you need new ideas, that doesn't mean you need to throw out the current stack. Progress has mostly come from adding things like RLHF, chain-of-thought, RL on verifiable tasks, tool use, and longer context to the same basic foundation. I'd expect continual learning and better long-horizon agency to arrive the same way, as additions rather than a total restart.

Third, and most important, there are a huge number of very smart people with enormous compute budgets working on exactly these limitations. If a new idea is needed, the question isn't whether we need it. It's how long it takes to find. Given the resources being poured in, and given that AI itself is starting to speed up AI research, I don't think a needed breakthrough implies a long delay. It might mean a couple of years instead of one, not decades.

And the trend lines matter here. If you look at measurements like the length of tasks AI agents can complete autonomously, that's been growing pretty steadily, doubling every several months. If there were a fundamental wall, you might expect that curve to bend. So far it hasn't, at least not obviously. It could, and I'm uncertain, which is why my timelines have a wide spread. But I'd say the burden of proof has shifted somewhat. Saying "current methods have limitations" isn't enough. You need to explain why those particular limitations won't fall to the same mix of scaling and incremental innovation that knocked down the previous ones.

So my overall take: maybe some new ingredients are needed, probably for things like sample-efficient online learning. But I don't think that buys us as much time as people hope, and I wouldn't plan around it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I take that argument seriously, but I don't find it very reassuring, for a couple of reasons.

The first is just the track record. If you go back five or ten years, there was a whole series of things people said would require a fundamentally new paradigm. Language models can't do reasoning, they can't do math, they can't write working code, they can't plan over long horizons. And each time, what actually happened was some combination of scale, better data, and relatively modest architectural or training innovations, like RLHF and then reasoning training with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks. Those weren't new paradigms in the sense critics meant. They were more like tweaks on top of the existing one. So when someone says "current models have limitation X, and that limitation will require a new paradigm," my prior is that it'll probably get patched by something less dramatic than they're imagining.

The second thing is: even if you grant that a new paradigm is needed, that doesn't tell you much about timelines unless you also think new paradigms are rare and slow to arrive. And I don't think that's obviously true anymore. There are hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into this field, the number of talented researchers has exploded, and increasingly the models themselves are helping with the research. If the key bottleneck really is some conceptual breakthrough in, say, continual learning or sample efficiency, there are a lot of people hunting for it, and they have a lot of compute to run experiments. So "we need a new idea" is compatible with "we get that new idea in two years."

Where I think the argument has the most force is on the specific gaps that look structural rather than incidental. The one I'd point to is long-horizon agency, the ability to work on a task for days or weeks, keep track of what you've learned, and not fall apart. Current models are weirdly spiky. They can be superhuman on some benchmarks and then fail at things a competent intern could do, because they don't really learn on the job the way humans do. Now, we're seeing the task horizon that models can handle doubling pretty steadily. So my best guess is that this gets solved incrementally rather than through some revolution. But I'll admit it's the place where I'm least confident, and if progress stalls, that's probably where it stalls.

So to sum up: I think the "new paradigm" framing is often a way of smuggling in long timelines without actually arguing for them. The honest version of the claim is "there are capabilities current methods haven't delivered yet," which is true, and then the real question is how fast the field is at closing that kind of gap. And the answer so far has been: faster than almost anyone expected. I'd love to be wrong about that, honestly, because it would give us more time to prepare. But I wouldn't plan around it.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated cases where capabilities once said to require a new paradigm—such as reasoning, math, coding, and planning—were achieved through scale, data, and modest changes to existing methods.

r002.rationale: It says those advances were not new paradigms in the sense critics meant, but does not identify relabeling an approach after it succeeds as moving the goalposts.

r003.rationale: The response mentions reasoning training as a past development, but does not say Kokotajlo predicted its near-term success or that it was later characterized as a new paradigm.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish two claims. One is that current models have important limitations. That seems clearly true. The other is that overcoming those limitations requires a fundamentally new paradigm, and I don’t think that follows.

You could look at a model failing at a task and say, “It just can’t reason.” But that doesn’t tell you whether the problem will persist with more training, better training data, or more time spent working through the problem. You need some argument for why those things won’t help, rather than just examples of failures today.

And “new paradigm” is a somewhat slippery phrase. If you take a pretrained model and train it to use tools, check its work, and learn from attempts at difficult tasks, does that count as a new paradigm? Someone might say yes, but it wouldn’t necessarily require a major scientific breakthrough or imply a long delay.

So I’m open to the possibility that we’ll hit a wall. I just wouldn’t feel comfortable relying on that. The question I’d want to ask is: What specific limitation do you expect to remain, and what evidence would change your mind?

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish two claims. One is that current models have important limitations. That seems clearly true. The other is that overcoming those limitations requires a fundamentally new paradigm, and I’m much less convinced of that.

When someone says “a new paradigm,” I want to ask what counts. Does adding a mechanism for models to check their work count? Does giving them more time to reason, or training them to use tools and learn from the results? Those could produce substantial improvements while preserving much of the current approach.

There’s also a difference between identifying a weakness and showing that it will persist. You can demonstrate that a model fails at some task, but that doesn’t establish that a larger model, or one trained differently, will fail in the same way. You need an argument for why the limitation is fundamental.

So I’m open to the possibility that we’ll need some major conceptual breakthrough. But I wouldn’t feel comfortable relying on that as a reason to expect long timelines. My view is that we should take seriously the possibility that the ingredients we already have, with further engineering and experimentation, are enough.
